arXiv:2403.15298v2 [math.CO] 23 Apr 2026

On the matching complexes of the categorical product of path graphs

Raju Kumar Gupta Address: Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, India Email address: rajukrg3217@gmail.com , Sourav Sarkar Address: Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, India Email address: sarkarsourav610@gmail.com , Sagar S. Sawant Address: Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, India Email address: sagar@smail.iitm.ac.in and Samir Shukla Address: School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Mandi, India Email address: samir@iitmandi.ac.in
Abstract.

The matching complex 𝖬⁡(G)\mathsf{M}(G) of a graph GG is a simplicial complex whose simplices are matchings in GG. These complexes appear in various places and found applications in many areas of mathematics including computational geometry, representation theory, combinatorics, etc. In this article, we consider the matching complexes of the categorical product Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} of path graphs PnP_{n} and PmP_{m}. For m=1m=1, Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} is a discrete graph and therefore its matching complex is the void complex. For m=2m=2, 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{m}) has been proved to be homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres by Kozlov. We show that for n≥2n\geq 2 and 3≤m≤53\leq m\leq 5, the matching complex of Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres. For m=3m=3, we explicitly compute the number and dimension of spheres appearing in the wedge. Furthermore, for m∈{4,5}m\in\{4,5\}, we provide the minimum and maximum dimensions of spheres appearing in the wedge in the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{m}).

Key words and phrases: 
matching complex, independence complex, categorical product of graphs, path graph, line graph
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
55P10, 05E45, 55U10

1 Introduction

A matching in a simple graph GG is a collection of pairwise disjoint edges. The matching complex 𝖬⁡(G)\mathsf{M}(G) of a graph GG is the simplicial complex whose vertices are the edges, and simplicies are the matchings in GG. In topological combinatorics, it is an important problem to study the topology of matching complexes of graphs. Matching complexes first appeared in the thesis of Garst [Gar79], where they obtained the matching complexes of complete bipartite graphs Km,nK_{m,n} as special coset complexes of symmetric groups SnS_{n}. Thereafter, matching complexes have appeared and found applications in various places. The matching complexes of complete graphs were studied in the paper of Bouc [Bou92] in connection with Brown complexes and Quillen complexes. In [BLVv94], Björner et al., described the matching complexes of complete bipartite graphs as chessboard complexes to study the geometry of non-attacking rook configurations on a general m×nm\times n chessboard. In [vV92], 𝖬⁡(Km,n)\mathsf{M}(K_{m,n}) appeared as the complex of all partial injective functions from {1,…,m}\{1,\ldots,m\} to {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\} in connection to the problem of estimating the number of halving hyperplanes of a finite set of points in Euclidean space. Other than the complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs, the classes of graphs for which matching complexes have been studied include; paths and cycles [Koz99], trees [MT08, MJMV22], polygonal tilings [Mat22, BJMV23], honeycomb graphs [MT08], etc. For more details on these complexes, we refer to a survey article by Wachs [Wac03] and Chapter 11 of the book [Jon08] by Jonsson.

Definition 1.1.

The cartesian product G​□​HG\Box H of graphs GG and HH is the graph with vertex set V⁡(G)×V⁡(H)V(G)\times V(H), where any two vertices (u,v)(u,v) and (u′,v′)(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}) form an edge if and only if either u=u′u=u^{\prime} and v​v′∈E⁡(H)vv^{\prime}\in E(H), or v=v′v=v^{\prime} and u​u′∈E⁡(G)uu^{\prime}\in E(G).

Definition 1.2.

The categorical product G×HG\times H of graphs GG and HH is the graph with vertex set V⁡(G)×V⁡(H)V(G)\times V(H), where any two vertices (u,v)(u,v) and (u′,v′)(u^{\prime},v^{\prime}) form an edge if and only if u​u′∈E⁡(G)uu^{\prime}\in E(G) and v​v′∈E⁡(H)vv^{\prime}\in E(H).

For n≥1n\geq 1, let PnP_{n} denote the path graph on nn vertices. The matching complexes of the cartesian product of path graphs have been studied by various authors. In [Koz99], Kozlov studied 𝖬⁡(Pn​□​P1)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\Box P_{1}). In [Jon05], Jonsson studied the homotopical depth and topological connectivity of matching complexes of the cartesian product of path graphs for certain cases. Furthermore, Braun and Hough investigated the homology of 𝖬⁡(Pn​□​P2)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\Box P_{2}) in [BH17], and its homotopy type was examined by Matsushita in [Mat19].

Motivated by the cartesian product of path graphs, in this article, we consider the matching complexes of the categorical product Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} of path graphs (see Figure 1). Since Pn×P1P_{n}\times P_{1} does not contain any edge, 𝖬⁡(Pn×P1)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{1}) is a void complex. Further, Pn×P2P_{n}\times P_{2} is a disjoint union of two path graphs, and therefore 𝖬⁡(Pn×P2)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{2}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres from [Koz99]. For 3≤m≤53\leq m\leq 5, we compute the homotopy type of the matching complexes of Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m}.

Theorem 1.3.

For n≥2n\geq 2 and 3≤m≤53\leq m\leq 5, 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{m}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

We explicitly compute the dimension and number of spheres in the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P3)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{3}) (see Theorem 3.5). For m∈{4,5}m\in\{4,5\}, we give the minimum and maximum dimension of spheres appearing in the wedge in homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{m}).

Proposition 1.4.

For n≥3n\geq 3, let dm​a​x​(𝖬⁡(Pn×P5))d_{max}(\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})) and dm​i​n​(𝖬⁡(Pn×P5))d_{min}(\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})) denote the maximum and minimum dimension of spheres appearing in the wedge in the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5}), respectively. Then, dm​a​x​(𝖬⁡(Pn×P5))d_{max}(\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})) and dm​i​n​(𝖬⁡(Pn×P5))d_{min}(\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})) are given in Table 1.

Proposition 1.5.

For n≥3n\geq 3, the minimum dimension of a sphere in the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P4)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{4}) is 2​k+12k+1 if n=2​k+2n=2k+2, and 2​k+32k+3 if n=2​k+3n=2k+3. The maximum dimension of a sphere in the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P4)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{4}) is given in Table 2.

The line graph L⁡(G)L(G) of a graph GG is the graph whose vertices are the edges of GG, and any two such distinct vertices u​vuv and u′​v′u^{\prime}v^{\prime} are joined by an edge in L⁡(G)L(G) if and only if they have a common endpoint, i.e., if {u,v}∩{u′,v′}≠∅\{u,v\}\cap\{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}\}\neq\emptyset. For a graph GG, a subset A⊆V⁡(G)A\subseteq V(G) is said to be independent in GG if the induced subgraph on AA does not contain any edge. The independence complex Ind⁡(G)\mathrm{Ind}(G) of GG is a simplicial complex on V⁡(G)V(G) whose simplices are the independent sets in GG. Observe that for any graph GG, the matching complex 𝖬⁡(G)\mathsf{M}(G) is the same as the Ind⁡(L⁡(G))\mathrm{Ind}(L(G)).

To prove Theorem 1.3, we show that Ind⁡(L⁡(Pn×Pm))\mathrm{Ind}(L(P_{n}\times P_{m})) is a wedge of spheres up to homotopy equivalence. The main idea used in this proof is to reduce the graph L⁡(Pn×Pm)L(P_{n}\times P_{m}) into smaller graphs by the operations; deletions of vertices, deletions of edges, and additions of edges. During this process of reduction, we come across thirteen new classes of graphs in the case m=5m=5, four new classes of graphs in the case m=4m=4, and one new class of graphs in the case m=3m=3. We establish recursive relations among the independence complex of L⁡(Pn×Pm)L(P_{n}\times P_{m}) and independence complexes of these new classes of graphs.

This paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we present the necessary preliminaries on graph theory and simplicial complexes. In Section 3, we determine the homotopy type of the matching complexes of Pn×P3P_{n}\times P_{3}, showing that it is a wedge of spheres, and we explicitly compute both the number and the dimensions of the spheres appearing in the wedge. In Section 4, we compute the homotopy type of the matching complexes of Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4}. The graph Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4} is disconnected and consists of two connected components. Regardless of whether nn is odd or even, these components are isomorphic. For n≥0n\geq 0, we denote the connected components of the line graphs of P2​n+2×P4P_{2n+2}\times P_{4} and P2​n+3×P4P_{2n+3}\times P_{4} by Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} (see Figure 4(a)) and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} (see Figure 4(b)), respectively. In Section 4.1, we formally define the graphs Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}, Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}, and four intermediary graphs needed to compute the homotopy types of the independence complexes of Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}. In Section 4.2, we establish recursive relations between their independence complexes. Then, in Section 4.3, we conclude the homotopy type of the matching complexes of Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4}, showing that it is a wedge of spheres, and we determine the maximum and minimum dimensions of spheres that occur in the wedge in 𝖬⁡(Pn×P4)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{4}).

Section 5 is majorly dedicated to the matching complexes of Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5} and is divided into three subsections. The graph L⁡(Pn×P5)L(P_{n}\times P_{5}) is disconnected and has exactly two components. For k≥0k\geq 0, if n=2​k+2n=2k+2, then L⁡(Pn×P5)L(P_{n}\times P_{5}) consists of two copies of the graph Γk,5\Gamma_{k,5} (see Figure 10); and if n=2​k+3n=2k+3, then L⁡(Pn×P5)=Λk,5⊔Γ~k,5L(P_{n}\times P_{5})=\Lambda_{k,5}\sqcup\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k,5} (see Figure 11 and Figure 12). We start Section 5 with the definitions of the graphs Γk,5,Λk,5\Gamma_{k,5},\Lambda_{k,5} and Γ~k,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k,5}. In Section 5.1, we compute the independence complexes of Γk,5\Gamma_{k,5} and Λk,5\Lambda_{k,5}. We introduce 66 new classes of graphs (which we need in the computation of Ind⁡(Γk,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{k,5}) and Ind⁡(Λk,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{k,5})), and establish recursive relations among independence complexes of graphs Γk,5,Λk,5\Gamma_{k,5},\Lambda_{k,5} and these 66 classes of graphs. In Section 5.2, we compute the independence complex of the graph Γ~k,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k,5}. Here again, we define another 77 class of graphs (which we need in the computation of Ind⁡(Γ~k,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k,5})), and establish recursive relations among independence complexes of these 77 new classes of graphs and Ind⁡(Γ~k,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k,5}). In Section 5.3, we conclude the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5}) and determine the minimum and maximum dimensions of spheres appearing in the wedge in 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5}). Finally, in Section 6, we pose a few questions and a conjecture, which naturally arise from the work done in this paper.

2 Preliminaries

A graph GG is an ordered pair (V⁡(G),E⁡(G))(V(G),E(G)), where V⁡(G)V(G) is a finite set of vertices and E⁡(G)⊆(V⁡(G)2)E(G)\subseteq\binom{V(G)}{2} is the set of edges of GG, consisting of 22-element subsets of V⁡(G)V(G). For the sake of brevity, we denote an edge {u,v}\{u,v\} by u​vuv. Given a graph G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)) and a vertex uu in V⁡(G)V(G), the open neighborhood of uu is defined as the collection {v∈V⁡(G):u​v∈E⁡(G)}\{v\in V(G):uv\in E(G)\} and it is denoted by N⁡(u)N(u). The closed neighborhood of a vertex uu in the graph GG is defined as {u}∪N⁡(u)\{u\}\cup N(u), and is denoted by N⁡[u]N[u]. A map f:V⁡(G)→V⁡(H)f\colon V(G)\rightarrow V(H) is said to be a graph homomorphism if f⁡(v)​f​(w)∈E⁡(H)f(v)f(w)\in E(H) for all v​w∈E⁡(G)vw\in E(G). A bijective graph homomorphism is called an isomorphism. If such an isomorphism exists between two graphs GG and HH, they are called isomorphic, denoted as G≅HG\cong H. Let S={v1,…,vr}S=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{r}\} be a collection of vertices in V⁡(G)V(G). Then, G∖SG\setminus S denotes the induced subgraph of GG on the vertex set V⁡(G)∖SV(G)\setminus S. In particular, if SS is the singleton set {v1}\{v_{1}\}, then we write the graph G∖SG\setminus S as G∖v1G\setminus v_{1}. Similarly, for a collection of edges T={e1,…,es}T=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{s}\}, by G+TG+T and G−TG-T we denote the graphs on the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) with edge set E⁡(G)∪TE(G)\cup T and E⁡(G)∖TE(G)\setminus T, respectively. For more details about the graphs, we refer the reader to [Wes01].

An (abstract) simplicial complex Δ\Delta on a vertex set VV is a collection of subsets of VV such that if σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta and τ\tau is a subset of σ\sigma, then τ∈Δ\tau\in\Delta. If σ∈Δ\sigma\in\Delta and |σ|=k+1|\sigma|=k+1, then we say σ\sigma is a simplex of dimension kk or a kk-simplex. We further assume that the empty set is present in every simplicial complex as the only simplex of dimension −1-1. The 00-dimensional simplices are called the vertices of Δ\Delta, and the set of all vertices of a simplicial complex Δ\Delta is denoted by V⁡(Δ)V(\Delta).

A subcomplex of a simplicial complex is a sub-collection of simplices that itself forms a simplicial complex. If Δ\Delta is a simplicial complex and σ\sigma is a simplex in Δ\Delta, then the link and deletion of σ\sigma are defined as the subcomplexes {τ∈Δ:σ∪τ∈Δ​and​σ∩τ=∅}\{\tau\in\Delta:\sigma\cup\tau\in\Delta\hskip 5.69046pt\text{and}\hskip 2.84544pt\sigma\cap\tau=\emptyset\} and {τ∈Δ:σ⊈τ}\{\tau\in\Delta:\sigma\nsubseteq\tau\}, respectively. The join of two simplicial complexes Δ1\Delta_{1} and Δ2\Delta_{2}, where V⁡(Δ1)∩V⁡(Δ2)=∅V(\Delta_{1})\cap V(\Delta_{2})=\emptyset, is the simplicial complex Δ1∗Δ2≔{σ∪τ:σ∈Δ1​and​τ∈Δ2}\Delta_{1}\ast\Delta_{2}\coloneq\{\sigma\cup\tau:\sigma\in\Delta_{1}\hskip 5.69046pt\text{and}\hskip 2.84544pt\tau\in\Delta_{2}\}. In particular, if a,ba,b are vertices that are not part of a simplicial complex Δ\Delta, then the simplicial complexes {a}∗Δ\{a\}\ast\Delta and ({a}∗Δ)∪({b}∗Δ)(\{a\}\ast\Delta)\cup(\{b\}\ast\Delta) are called the cone and the suspension of Δ\Delta with the apexes aa and {a,b}\{a,b\}, respectively. We denote the suspension of Δ\Delta with apex {a,b}\{a,b\} by Σa,b​Δ\Sigma_{a,b}\Delta (or Σ​Δ\Sigma\Delta).

In this article, we consider any simplicial complex as a topological space, namely its geometric realization. For the definition of geometric realization, we refer the reader to [Koz08]. For details about topological background, one may refer to [Hat02].

Proposition 2.1.

Let G1⊔G2G_{1}\sqcup G_{2} denote the disjoint union of two graphs, G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}. Then Ind⁡(G1⊔G2)≃Ind⁡(G1)∗Ind⁡(G2).\mathrm{Ind}(G_{1}\sqcup G_{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(G_{1})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(G_{2}).

Clearly, for each vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), the link and the deletion of the simplex {v}\{v\} in Ind⁡(G)\mathrm{Ind}(G) are the same as Ind⁡(G∖N⁡[v])\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[v]) and Ind⁡(G∖v)\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus v), respectively. Observe that Ind⁡(G)\mathrm{Ind}(G) is the same as the simplicial complex ({v}∗Ind⁡(G∖N⁡[v]))∪Ind⁡(G∖v)(\{v\}\ast\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[v]))\cup\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus v). Further, from [Ada12], we have the following:

Proposition 2.2 (Proposition 3.1, [Ada12]).

Let vv be a vertex of a graph GG. If the inclusion Ind⁡(G∖N⁡[v])↪Ind⁡(G∖v)\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[v])\xhookrightarrow{}\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus v) is null-homotopic, then we have

Ind⁡(G)≃Ind⁡(G∖v)∨Σ​Ind​(G∖N⁡[v]).\mathrm{Ind}(G)\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus v)\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[v]).
Proposition 2.3 (Lemma 2.4, [Eng08]).

Let vv and ww be a pair of distinct vertices of GG with N⁡(v)⊆N⁡(w)N(v)\subseteq N(w). Then Ind⁡(G)≃Ind⁡(G∖w)\mathrm{Ind}(G)\simeq{}\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus w).

Proposition 2.4 (Lemma 2.5, [Eng08]).

Let GG be a graph and vv be a simplicial vertex of GG, that is, all neighbors of vv are pairwise adjacent. Let N⁡(v)={w1,w2,…,wk}N(v)=\{w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{k}\}. Then Ind⁡(G)≃⋁i=1kΣ​Ind​(G∖N⁡[wi]).\mathrm{Ind}(G)\simeq\bigvee_{i=1}^{k}\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[w_{i}]).

Proposition 2.5 (Proposition 3.4, [Ada12]).

Let GG be a graph and let u​vuv be an edge in GG. If Ind⁡(G∖N⁡[u,v])\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[u,v]) is contractible, then Ind⁡(G)≃Ind⁡(G∖u​v).\mathrm{Ind}(G)\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus uv).

Definition 2.6.

A triplet of distinct vertices u,vu,v and xx in a graph GG satisfying x∉N⁡(u)∪N⁡(v)x\notin N(u)\cup N(v) and N⁡(x)⊆N⁡(u)∪N⁡(v)N(x)\subseteq N(u)\cup N(v) is called an edge-invariant triplet in GG, and denoted by [u,v;x][u,v;x].

Based on the Proposition 2.5, we have the following. Suppose GG is a graph that consists of vertices {u,v}\{u,v\} and some vertex xx (depending on uu and vv) such that [u,v;x][u,v;x] is an edge invariant triplet in GG. Then xx is an isolated vertex in G∖N⁡[u,v]G\setminus N[u,v], which implies that Ind⁡(G∖N⁡[u,v])\mathrm{Ind}(G\setminus N[u,v]) is contractible. Thus, we have

Ind⁡(G)≃Ind⁡(G​△​u​v),\mathrm{Ind}(G)\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(G\triangle uv),

where V⁡(G​△​u​v)=V⁡(G)V(G\triangle uv)=V(G), and E⁡(G​△​u​v)E(G\triangle uv) is given by the symmetric difference E⁡(G)​△​{u​v}.E(G)\triangle\{uv\}.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the path graph PnP_{n} is a graph with V⁡(Pn)={vi∣1≤i≤n}V(P_{n})=\{v_{i}\mid 1\leq i\leq n\} and E⁡(Pn)={vi​vi+1∣1≤i≤n−1}E(P_{n})=\{v_{i}v_{i+1}\mid 1\leq i\leq n-1\}.

Proposition 2.7 (Proposition 4.6, [Koz99]).

For n≥1n\geq 1,

Ind⁡(Pn)≃{𝕊k−1if​n=3​k,3​k−1,a pointif​n=3​k+1.\mathrm{Ind}(P_{n})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{k-1}&\text{if}\ n=3k,3k-1,\\ \text{a point}&\text{if}\ n=3k+1.\\ \end{cases}

For n≥1n\geq 1, the cycle graph 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} is a graph with V⁡(𝒞n)={vi∣1≤i≤n}V(\mathcal{C}_{n})=\{v_{i}\mid 1\leq i\leq n\} and E⁡(𝒞n)={vi​vi+1∣1≤i≤n−1}∪{v1​vn}E(\mathcal{C}_{n})=\{v_{i}v_{i+1}\mid 1\leq i\leq n-1\}\cup\{v_{1}v_{n}\}.

Proposition 2.8 (Proposition 5.2, [Koz99]).

For n≥3n\geq 3,

Ind⁡(𝒞n)≃{𝕊k−1∨Sk−1if​n=3​k,𝕊k−1if​n=3​k±1.\mathrm{Ind}(\mathcal{C}_{n})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\vee S^{k-1}&\text{if}\ n=3k,\\ \mathbb{S}^{k-1}&\text{if}\ n=3k\pm 1.\\ \end{cases}

3 Matching complexes of Pn×P3P_{n}\times P_{3}

In this section, we determine the homotopy type of the matching complex of Pn×P3P_{n}\times P_{3}. The graph Pn×P3P_{n}\times P_{3} is disconnected and has two connected components. When nn is even, then these components are isomorphic. However, for nn odd, the components are not isomorphic. For n≥0n\geq 0, we denote the (isomorphic) connected components of the line graphs of P2​n+2×P3P_{2n+2}\times P_{3} by Γn,3\Gamma_{n,3} (see Figure 2(a)). Furthermore, for n≥0n\geq 0, we denote the (non-isomorphic) connected components of the line graphs of P2​n+3×P3P_{2n+3}\times P_{3} by Λn,3\Lambda_{n,3} and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3} (see Figures 3(a) and 3(b)), respectively. Therefore, we have the following:

𝖬⁡(P2​n+2×P3)≃Ind⁡(Γn,3)∗Ind⁡(Γn,3)​and​𝖬​(P2​n+3×P3)≃Ind⁡(Λn,3)∗Ind⁡(Γ~n,3).\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+2}\times P_{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})*\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\ \text{and}\ \mathsf{M}(P_{2n+3}\times P_{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})*\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3}).

During the computation of the homotopy type of the independence complexes of graphs Γn,3,Λn,3\Gamma_{n,3},\Lambda_{n,3}, and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3} for n≥0n\geq 0, we encounter an intermediary graph, denoted as An,3A_{n,3} (see Figure 2(b)). Using the independence complex of An,3A_{n,3}, we illustrate that the independence complexes of Γn,3,Λn,3\Gamma_{n,3},\Lambda_{n,3}, and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3} are the wedges of spheres.

(i) Graph Γn,3\Gamma_{n,3}
For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph Γn,3\Gamma_{n,3} as follows:

V⁡(Γn,3)={gi​j:i=1,2 and j=1,2,…,2n+1},E⁡(Γn,3)={g1​jg2​j:j=1,2,…,2n+1}∪{gi​jgi​j+1:i=1,2 and j=1,2,…,2n}∪{g1​jg2​j+1,g1​j+1g2​j:j=2,4,…,2n}.\begin{split}V(\Gamma_{n,3})=&\{g_{ij}:i=1,2\text{ and }j={1,2,\dots,2n{+}1}\},\\ E(\Gamma_{n,3})=&\ \{g_{1j}g_{2j}:j=1,2,\dots,2n{+}1\}\cup\{g_{ij}g_{i\,j+1}:i=1,2\text{ and }j=1,2,\dots,2n\}\\ &\cup\{g_{1j}g_{2\,j+1},g_{1\,j+1}g_{2\,j}:\;j=2,4,\dots,2n\}.\end{split}
Claim 3.1.

For n≥0n\geq 0, Ind⁡(Γn,3)≃𝕊n\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{n}.

Proof.

Since N⁡(g11)⊆N⁡(g22)N(g_{11})\subseteq N(g_{22}) in Γn,3\Gamma_{n,3} and N⁡(g21)⊆N⁡(g12)N(g_{21})\subseteq N(g_{12}) in Γn,3∖g22\Gamma_{n,3}\setminus g_{22}, using Proposition 2.3, we get that Ind⁡(Γn,3)≃Ind⁡(Γn,3∖{g12,g22}).\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3}\setminus\{g_{12},g_{22}\}). It is straightforward to see that Γn,3∖{g12,g22}\Gamma_{n,3}\setminus\{g_{12},g_{22}\} has two connected components; one component is an edge g11​g21g_{11}g_{21}, and the other is isomorphic to Γn−1,3\Gamma_{n-1,3}. Therefore, Ind⁡(Γn,3)≃Σ​Ind​(Γn−1,3)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n-1,3}). Consequently, we get Ind⁡(Γn,3)≃Σn​Ind​(Γ0,3).\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\simeq\Sigma^{n}\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{0,3}). Since Γ0,3≅K2\Gamma_{0,3}\cong K_{2}, the result follows by induction. ∎

(ii) Graph An,3A_{n,3}
For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph An,3A_{n,3} as follows:

V⁡(An,3)=V⁡(Γn,3)∪{a1}V(A_{n,3})=V(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{a_{1}\} and E⁡(An,3)=E⁡(Γn,3)∪{a1​g11,a1​g21}.E(A_{n,3})=E(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{a_{1}g_{11},a_{1}g_{21}\}.

Claim 3.2.

For n≥0n\geq 0, Ind⁡(An,3)≃⋁2Σ​Ind​(An−1,3)≃⋁2n+1𝕊n.\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2}\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n+1}}\mathbb{S}^{n}.

Proof.

Since a1a_{1} is a simplicial vertex in the graph An,3A_{n,3} (see Figure 2(b)) with N⁡(a1)={g11,g21}N(a_{1})=\{g_{11},g_{21}\}, from Proposition 2.4, we have Ind⁡(An,3)≃Σ​Ind​(An,3∖N⁡[g11])∨Σ​Ind​(An,3∖N⁡[g21]).\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{11}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{21}]). Since both the graphs An,3∖N⁡[g11]A_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{11}] and An,3∖N⁡[g21]A_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{21}] are isomorphic to An−1,3A_{n-1,3}, we have Ind⁡(An,3)≃⋁2Σ​Ind​(An−1,3)\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2}\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,3}). Proceeding in this way for nn steps, we obtain Ind⁡(An,3)≃⋁2nΣn​Ind​(A0,3)\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n}}\Sigma^{n}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{0,3}). Observe that the graph A0,3A_{0,3} is isomorphic to K3K_{3}, and hence Ind⁡(A0,3)≃𝕊0∨𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(A_{0,3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0}\vee\mathbb{S}^{0}. Therefore, Ind⁡(An,3)≃⋁2nΣn​(𝕊0∨𝕊0)≃⋁2n(𝕊n∨Sn)\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,3})\simeq{\bigvee}^{2^{n}}\Sigma^{n}(\mathbb{S}^{0}\vee\mathbb{S}^{0})\simeq{\bigvee}^{2^{n}}(\mathbb{S}^{n}\vee S^{n}). This completes the proof. ∎

(iii) Graphs Λn,3\Lambda_{n,3} and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3}
For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graphs Λn,3\Lambda_{n,3} (see Figure 3(a)) and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3} (see Figure 3(b)) as follows:

V⁡(Λn,3)=V⁡(Γn,3)∪{g1′,g2′}V(\Lambda_{n,3})=V(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{g^{\prime}_{1},g^{\prime}_{2}\}, E⁡(Λn,3)=E⁡(Γn,3)∪{g1′​g11,g2′​g21,g1′​g2′,g1′​g21,g2′​g11}E(\Lambda_{n,3})=E(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{g^{\prime}_{1}g_{11},g^{\prime}_{2}g_{21},g^{\prime}_{1}g^{\prime}_{2},g^{\prime}_{1}g_{21},g^{\prime}_{2}g_{11}\}, and

V⁡(Γ~n,3)=V⁡(Γn,3)∪{g12​n+2,g22​n+2},E⁡(Γ~n,3)=E⁡(Γn,3)∪{g12​n+1​g12​n+2,g22​n+1​g22​n+2,g12​n+2​g22​n+2}.\begin{split}V(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3})=&V(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{g_{12n+2},g_{22n+2}\},\\ E(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3})=&E(\Gamma_{n,3})\cup\{g_{12n+1}g_{12n+2},g_{22n+1}g_{22n+2},g_{12n+2}g_{22n+2}\}.\end{split}
Claim 3.3.

For n≥0n\geq 0, Ind⁡(Λn,3)≃⋁2n+2−1𝕊n.\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n+2}-1}\mathbb{S}^{n}.

Proof.

The proof is by induction on nn. Clearly, Ind⁡(Λ0,3)≃⋁3𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{0,3})\simeq\bigvee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{0}. Assume that n≥1n\geq 1 and the Claim 3.3 holds for all 0≤k<n0\leq k<n. Since g1′g^{\prime}_{1} is a simplicial vertex and N⁡(g1′)={g2′,g11,g21}N(g^{\prime}_{1})=\{g^{\prime}_{2},g_{11},g_{21}\} in the graph Λn,3\Lambda_{n,3} (see Figure 3(a)), from Proposition 2.4, we have

Ind⁡(Λn,3)≃Σ​Ind​(Λn,3∖N⁡[g2′])∨Σ​Ind​(Λn,3∖N⁡[g11])∨Σ​Ind​(Λn,3∖N⁡[g21]).\begin{split}\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})&\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g^{\prime}_{2}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{11}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{21}]).\end{split}

Observe that, the graph Λn,3∖N⁡[g2′]\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g^{\prime}_{2}] is isomorphic to Λn−1,3\Lambda_{n-1,3}, whereas both the graphs Λn,3∖N⁡[g11]\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{11}] and Λn,3∖N⁡[g21]\Lambda_{n,3}\setminus N[g_{21}] are isomorphic to An−1,3A_{n-1,3}. Therefore, we get

Ind⁡(Λn,3)≃Σ​Ind​(Λn−1,3)∨Σ​Ind​(An−1,3)∨Σ​Ind​(An−1,3).\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n-1,3})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,3})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,3}).

Now, from the induction hypothesis and Claim 3.2, we conclude that Ind⁡(Λn,3)≃⋁2n+2−1𝕊n\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n+2}-1}\mathbb{S}^{n} ∎

Claim 3.4.

For n≥0n\geq 0, Ind⁡(Γ~n,3)≃𝕊n\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{n}.

Proof.

The proof for Ind⁡(Γ~n,3)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3}) is essentially verbatim to the proof of Claim 3.1. ∎

Theorem 3.5.

For n≥0n\geq 0, 𝖬⁡(P2​n+2×P3)≃𝕊2​n+1\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+2}\times P_{3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{2n+1} and 𝖬⁡(P2​n+3×P3)≃⋁2n+2−1𝕊2​n+1.\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+3}\times P_{3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n+2}-1}\mathbb{S}^{2n+1}.

Proof.

Since the line graph of the categorical product P2​n+2×P3P_{2n+2}\times P_{3} is the disjoint union of two copies of Γn,3\Gamma_{n,3}, using Proposition 2.1 and Claim 3.1, we get 𝖬⁡(P2​n+2×P3)≃Ind⁡(Γn,3)∗Ind⁡(Γn,3)≃𝕊2​n+1.\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+2}\times P_{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{2n+1}. Similarly, the line graph of the categorical product P2​n+3×P3P_{2n+3}\times P_{3} is the disjoint union of Λn,3\Lambda_{n,3} and Γ~n,3\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3}. Therefore, using Proposition 2.1, Claims 3.3 and 3.4 we get 𝖬⁡(P2​n+3×P3)≃Ind⁡(Λn,3)∗Ind⁡(Γ~n,3)≃⋁2n+2−1𝕊2​n+1.\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+3}\times P_{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,3})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,3})\simeq\bigvee^{2^{n+2}-1}\mathbb{S}^{2n+1}. ∎

4 Matching complexes of Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4}

In this section, we aim to determine the homotopy type of the matching complex of the categorical product Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4}. The graph Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4} is disconnected, and contains two connected components. Regardless of whether nn is odd or even, these respective components are isomorphic. For n≥0n\geq 0, we denote the connected components of the line graphs of P2​n+2×P4P_{2n+2}\times P_{4} and P2​n+3×P4P_{2n+3}\times P_{4} by Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} (see Figure 4(a)) and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} (see Figure 4(b)), respectively. Therefore, we have the following:

𝖬⁡(P2​n+2×P4)≃Ind⁡(Γn,4)∗Ind⁡(Γn,4),\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+2}\times P_{4})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4})*\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}),
𝖬⁡(P2​n+3×P4)≃Ind⁡(Γ~n,4)∗Ind⁡(Γ~n,4).\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+3}\times P_{4})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})*\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}).

During the computation of the homotopy type of the independence complexes of graphs Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} for n≥0n\geq 0, we encounter several intermediary graphs denoted as An,4,A~n,4,Bn,4A_{n,4},\widetilde{A}_{n,4},B_{n,4}, and B~n,4\widetilde{B}_{n,4}. We show that the independence complexes of Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} are wedges of suspensions of these intermediary graphs. By induction on nn, we show that the independence complexes of Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}, Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}, and the intermediary graphs are homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres. The graphs An,4,A~n,4,Bn,4A_{n,4},\widetilde{A}_{n,4},B_{n,4}, and B~n,4\widetilde{B}_{n,4} are shown in Figures 5(a), 5(b), 6 and 7, respectively. In the following subsection, we define the graphs Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}, Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}, along with four intermediary graphs. In the subsequent subsections, we then determine the homotopy types of the independence complexes of Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}, Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}, and these intermediary graphs.

4.1  Definitions of Graphs Γn,4,Γ~n,4\Gamma_{n,4},\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} and Other Intermediary Graphs

(i) Graph Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(Γn,4)={gi​j:i=1,2,3 and j=1,2,…,2n+1},E⁡(Γn,4)={gi​jgi+1​j:i=1,2 and j=1,2,…,2n+1}∪{gi​jgi​j+1:i=1,2,3 and j=1,2,…,2n}∪{gi​jgi+1​j+1,gi​j+1gi+1​j:i=1,2,j=1,2,…,2n, and i+j≡1(mod  2)}.\begin{split}V(\Gamma_{n,4})=&\{g_{ij}:i=1,2,3\ \text{ and }j={1,2,\dots,2n{+}1}\},\\ E(\Gamma_{n,4})=&\ \{g_{ij}g_{i+1\,j}:i=1,2\text{ and }j=1,2,\dots,2n{+}1\}\cup\{g_{ij}g_{i\,j+1}:i=1,2,3\text{ and }j=1,2,\dots,2n\}\\ &\cup\{g_{ij}g_{i+1\,j+1},g_{ij+1}g_{i+1\,j}:i=1,2,\;j=1,2,\dots,2n,\text{ and }i+j\equiv 1\,({\mathrm{mod\;\,}2})\}.\end{split}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(Γ~n,4)=V⁡(Γn,4)∪{g1 2​n+2,g2 2​n+2,g3 2​n+2},E⁡(Γ~n,4)=E⁡(Γn,4)∪{g1 2​n+2​g2 2​n+2,g2 2​n+2​g3 2​n+2,g1 2​n+1​g1 2​n+2}∪{g2 2​n+1​g2 2​n+2,g3 2​n+1​g3 2​n+2,g2 2​n+2​g3 2​n+1,g3 2​n+2​g2 2​n+1}.\begin{split}V(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})=&V(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{g_{1\,2n+2},g_{2\,2n+2},g_{3\,2n+2}\},\\ E(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})=&E(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{g_{1\,2n+2}g_{2\,2n+2},g_{2\,2n+2}g_{3\,2n+2},g_{1\,2n+1}g_{1\,2n+2}\}\\ &\cup\{g_{2\,2n+1}g_{2\,2n+2},g_{3\,2n+1}g_{3\,2n+2},g_{2\,2n+2}g_{3\,2n+1},g_{3\,2n+2}g_{2\,2n+1}\}.\end{split}

(iii) Graph An,4A_{n,4}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph An,4A_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(An,4)=V⁡(Γn,4)∪{a1}V(A_{n,4})=V(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{a_{1}\} and E⁡(An,4)=E⁡(Γn,4)∪{a1​g11,a1​g21}.E(A_{n,4})=E(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{a_{1}g_{11},a_{1}g_{21}\}.

(iv) Graph A~n,4\widetilde{A}_{n,4}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph A~n,4\widetilde{A}_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(A~n,4)=V⁡(Γ~n,4)∪{a1}V(\widetilde{A}_{n,4})=V(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\cup\{a_{1}\} and E⁡(A~n,4)=E⁡(Γ~n,4)∪{a1​g11,a1​g21}.E(\widetilde{A}_{n,4})=E(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\cup\{a_{1}g_{11},a_{1}g_{21}\}.

(v) Graph Bn,4B_{n,4}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph Bn,4B_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(Bn,4)=V⁡(Γn,4)∪{b1}V(B_{n,4})=V(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{b_{1}\} and E⁡(Bn,4)=E⁡(Γn,4)∪{b1​g11,b1​g21,b1​g31}E(B_{n,4})=E(\Gamma_{n,4})\cup\{b_{1}g_{11},b_{1}g_{21},b_{1}g_{31}\}.

(vi) Graph B~n,4\widetilde{B}_{n,4}

For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the graph B~n,4\widetilde{B}_{n,4} as follows:

V⁡(B~n,4)=V⁡(Γ~n,4)∪{b1}V(\widetilde{B}_{n,4})=V(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\cup\{b_{1}\} and E⁡(B~n,4)=E⁡(Γ~n,4)∪{b1​g11,b1​g21,b1​g31}E(\widetilde{B}_{n,4})=E(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\cup\{b_{1}g_{11},b_{1}g_{21},b_{1}g_{31}\}.

4.2  Independence complexes of Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4} and Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}

In this section, we establish recursive relations among the independence complexes of the graphs in {Γn,4,Γ~n,4,An,4,A~n,4,Bn,4,B~n,4}\{\Gamma_{n,4},\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4},A_{n,4},\widetilde{A}_{n,4},B_{n,4},\widetilde{B}_{n,4}\}.

Claim 4.1.

For n≥0n\geq 0,

Ind⁡(Γn,4)≃{𝕊0if n=0,𝕊1∨𝕊1if n=1,Σ​Ind​(An−1,4)∨Σ2​Ind​(Γ~n−2,4)if n≥2.\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{0}&\text{if $n=0$,}\\ \mathbb{S}^{1}\vee\mathbb{S}^{1}&\text{if $n=1$,}\\ \Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,4})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n-2,4})&\text{if $n\geq 2$.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Since Γ0,4\Gamma_{0,4} is a path on three vertices (see Figure 4(a)), from Proposition 2.7, we get Ind⁡(Γ0,4)≃𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{0,4})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0}. Now, consider n≥1n\geq 1. Since N⁡(g11)⊆N⁡(g22)N(g_{11})\subseteq N(g_{22}) in the graph Γn,4\Gamma_{n,4}, we have Ind⁡(Γn,4)≃Ind⁡(Γn,4∖g22)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}\setminus g_{22}). Let Γn,41≔Γn,4∖g22\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\coloneq\Gamma_{n,4}\setminus g_{22}. Since g31g_{31} is a simplicial vertex in Γn,41\Gamma_{n,4}^{1} with N⁡(g31)={g21,g32}N(g_{31})=\{g_{21},g_{32}\}, Proposition 2.4 implies that Ind⁡(Γn,41)≃Σ​Ind​(Γn,41∖N⁡[g21])∨Σ​Ind​(Γn,41∖N⁡[g32])\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{21}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}]). Observe that the graph Γn,41∖N⁡[g21]\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{21}] is isomorphic to An−1,4A_{n-1,4} (see Figure 5(a)). Therefore, Ind⁡(Γn,41)≃Σ​Ind​(An−1,4)∨Σ​Ind​(Γn,41∖N⁡[g32])\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,4})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}]). In case of n=1n=1, the graph Γ1,41∖N⁡[g32]\Gamma_{1,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}] is isomorphic to A0,4A_{0,4} (see Figure 5(a)). Therefore, Ind⁡(Γ1,41)≃Σ​Ind​(A0,4)∨Σ​Ind​(A0,4)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{1,4}^{1})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{0,4})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{0,4}). Using Claim 4.3, we get Ind⁡(Γ1,4)≃𝕊1∨𝕊1\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{1,4})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1}\vee\mathbb{S}^{1}.

Now, consider n≥2n\geq 2. Since g11g_{11} is a simplicial vertex and g12g_{12} is the only neighbor of g11g_{11} in the graph Γn,41∖N⁡[g32]\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}], we get Ind⁡(Γn,41∖N⁡[g32])≃Σ​Ind​(Γn,41∖N⁡[g32,g12])\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}])\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32},g_{12}]). Observe that the graph Γn,41∖N⁡[g32,g12]\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32},g_{12}] is isomorphic to Γ~n−2,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n-2,4} ( see Figure 4(b)) and therefore Ind⁡(Γn,41∖N⁡[g32])≃Σ​Ind​(Γ~n−2,4)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4}^{1}\setminus N[g_{32}])\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n-2,4}). Thus, Ind⁡(Γn,4)≃Σ​Ind​(An−1,4)∨Σ2​Ind​(Γ~n−2,4)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,4})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,4})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n-2,4}). ∎

Claim 4.2.

For n≥0n\geq 0,

Ind⁡(Γ~n,4)≃{𝕊1if n=0,∨3𝕊2if n=1,Σ​Ind​(A~n−1,4)∨Σ2​Ind​(Γn−2,4)if n≥2.\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{1}&\text{if $n=0$,}\\ \vee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{2}&\text{if $n=1$,}\\ \Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{A}_{n-1,4})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n-2,4})&\text{if $n\geq 2$.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Since N⁡(g11)⊆N⁡(g22)N(g_{11})\subseteq N(g_{22}) in the graph Γ~n,4\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4} (see Figure 4(b)), Ind⁡(Γ~n,4)≃Ind⁡(Γ~n,4∖g22)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,4}\setminus g_{22}). If n=0n=0, then N⁡(g12)⊆N⁡(g21)N(g_{12})\subseteq N(g_{21}) in Γ~0,4∖g22\widetilde{\Gamma}_{0,4}\setminus g_{22}. Hence Ind⁡(Γ~0,4)≃Ind⁡(Γ~0,4∖{g21,g22})\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{0,4})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{0,4}\setminus\{g_{21},g_{22}\}). Now, Γ~0,4∖{g21,g22}\widetilde{\Gamma}_{0,4}\setminus\{g_{21},g_{22}\} is the disjoint union of two edges g11​g12g_{11}g_{12} and g31​g32g_{31}g_{32}. In this section, we compute the homotopy type of the matching complex of the categorical product Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5}. Since PnP_{n} is bipartite, Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5} (and its line graph) is disconnected and contains exactly two connected components. When nn is even, these components are isomorphic; whereas, for odd nn, they are non-isomorphic.

For n≥0n\geq 0, we denote the connected component of the line graph of P2​n+2×P5P_{2n+2}\times P_{5} by Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5} (see Figure 10). Since the line graph L⁡(P2​n+2×P5)L(P_{2n+2}\times P_{5}) is the same as Γn,5⊔Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5}\sqcup\Gamma_{n,5}, the matching complex

𝖬⁡(P2​n+2×P5)=Ind⁡(L⁡(P2​n+2×P5))≃Ind⁡(Γn,5)∗Ind⁡(Γn,5).\mathsf{M}(P_{2n+2}\times P_{5})=\mathrm{Ind}(L(P_{2n+2}\times P_{5}))\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5})*\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5}).

Similarly, for n≥0n\geq 0, let Λn,5\Lambda_{n,5} and Γ~n,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5} (see Figures 11 and 12) denote the two non-isomorphic connected components of the line graph of P2​n+3×P5P_{2n+3}\times P_{5}. Therefore, we have

∪{gi​jgi​j+1|i=1,2,3,4andj=1,2,…,2n}\displaystyle\cup\{g_{ij}g_{i\,j+1}\;|\;i=1,2,3,4\ \text{and}\ j=1,2,\dots,2n\}

5.1  Independence complexes of Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5} and Λn,5\Lambda_{n,5}

In this section, we introduce 66 new classes of graphs, namely An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,Dn,5,A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5},D_{n,5}, En,5E_{n,5}, and Fn,5F_{n,5} for n≥0n\geq 0. We show that the independence complexes of Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5} and Λn,5\Lambda_{n,5} can be expressed in terms of wedges of suspensions of independence complexes of these intermediary graphs. Using induction on nn, we establish that the independence complexes of Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5}, Λn,5\Lambda_{n,5}, and these intermediary graphs are homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

We begin with the description of the intermediary graphs.

Claim 5.4.

Claim 5.5.
Ind⁡(Λn,5)≃{∨7𝕊1if n=0,(⋁2Σ2​Ind​(An−1,5))∨(⋁2Σ2​Ind​(Cn−1,5))∨(⋁2Σ2​Ind​(Fn−1,5))∨Σ2​Ind​(Dn−1,5)if n≥1.\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\vee^{7}\mathbb{S}^{1}&\text{if $n=0$,}\\ \left({\bigvee}^{2}\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,5})\right)\vee\left({\bigvee}^{2}\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n-1,5})\right)\vee\left({\bigvee}^{2}\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(F_{n-1,5})\right)\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n-1,5})&\text{if $n\geq 1$.}\end{cases}

First, let n=0n=0. Observe that the graphs Λ0,5∖N⁡[g21]\Lambda_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{21}] and Λ0,5∖N⁡[l2]\Lambda_{0,5}\setminus N[l_{2}] are isomorphic to the complete graph K3K_{3} and the graph Λ0,5∖N⁡[g11]\Lambda_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{11}] is isomorphic to the complete graph K4K_{4}. Therefore, Ind(Λ0,5)≃ΣInd(K3)∨ΣInd(K3)∨ΣInd(K4)≃∨7𝕊1.\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{0,5})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(K_{3})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(K_{3})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(K_{4})\simeq\vee^{7}\mathbb{S}^{1}.

Now, assume that n≥1n\geq 1. Note that Λn,5∖N⁡[l2]\Lambda_{n,5}\setminus N[l_{2}] is isomorphic to Cn+1,55C_{n+1,5}^{5} (see Figure 23(d) in Claim 5.8). Therefore, it follows from (5.9) that

(5.4) Ind⁡(Λn,5∖N⁡[l2])≃Σ​Ind​(An−1,5)∨Σ​Ind​(Fn−1,5).{}\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5}\setminus N[l_{2}])\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-1,5})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(F_{n-1,5}).

Since l4l_{4} is a simplicial vertex in Λn,51\Lambda_{n,5}^{1} with N⁡(l4)={l3,g31,g41}N(l_{4})=\{l_{3},g_{31},g_{41}\}, using Proposition 2.4, we have

Ind⁡(Λn,51)≃Σ​Ind​(Λn,51∖N⁡[l3])∨Σ​Ind​(Λn,51∖N⁡[g31])∨Σ​Ind​(Λn,51∖N⁡[g41]).\begin{split}\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5}^{1})&\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[l_{3}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{31}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{41}]).\end{split}

Observe that the graphs Λn,51∖N⁡[l3]\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[l_{3}], Λn,51∖N⁡[g31]\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{31}], and Λn,51∖N⁡[g41]\Lambda_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{41}] are isomorphic to the graphs Fn−1,5F_{n-1,5}, Cn−1,5C_{n-1,5} and Dn−1,5D_{n-1,5}, respectively (see Figure 18, 15 and 16 respectively). Further, for the simplicial vertex l3l_{3} with N⁡(l3)={l4,g41}N(l_{3})=\{l_{4},g_{41}\} in Λn,52\Lambda_{n,5}^{2}, we have

Ind⁡(An,5)≃{∨3𝕊1if n=0,Σ2​Ind​(Cn−1,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(Cn−1,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(Dn−1,5)if n≥1.\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\vee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{1}&\ \ \text{if $n=0$,}\\ \Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n-1,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n-1,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n-1,5})&\ \ \text{if $n\geq 1$.}\\ \end{cases}

Therefore, Proposition 2.4 provides us with

Ind⁡(An,5)≃Σ2​Ind​(An,5∖N⁡[g11,g31])\displaystyle\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,5})\simeq\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,5}\setminus N[g_{11},g_{31}]) ∨Σ2​Ind​(An,5∖N⁡[g11,g41])∨Σ2​Ind​(An,5∖N⁡[g21,g41]).\displaystyle\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,5}\setminus N[g_{11},g_{41}])\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n,5}\setminus N[g_{21},g_{41}]).

Claim 5.7.
Ind⁡(Bn,5)≃{𝕊1∨𝕊2if n=0,Σ​Ind​(Cn,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(Λn−1,5)if n≥1.\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{1}\vee\mathbb{S}^{2}&\ \ \text{if \ $n=0$},\\ \Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n-1,5})&\ \ \text{if \ $n\geq 1$}.\end{cases}
Proof.

First, let n=0n=0. Since g41g_{41} is a simplicial vertex in B0,5B_{0,5} with N⁡(g41)={g31,b5,b6}N(g_{41})=\{g_{31},b_{5},b_{6}\}, (see Figure 14), using Proposition 2.4, we get Ind⁡(B0,5)≃Σ​Ind​(B0,5∖N⁡[g31])∨Σ​Ind​(B0,5∖N⁡[b6])∨Σ​Ind​(B0,5∖N⁡[b5])\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{6}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{5}]). Now, b2b_{2} is an isolated vertex in the graph B0,5∖N⁡[b5]B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{5}]. Therefore, Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[b5])\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{5}]) is contractible. Since N⁡(b2)⊆N⁡(b4)N(b_{2})\subseteq N(b_{4}) in the graph B0,5∖N⁡[g31]B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}], using Proposition 2.5 we get Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[g31])≃Ind⁡(B0,5∖(N⁡[g31]∪{b4}))\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}])\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus(N[g_{31}]\cup\{b_{4}\})). Since the graph B0,5∖(N⁡[g31]∪{b4})B_{0,5}\setminus(N[g_{31}]\cup\{b_{4}\}) consists of two disjoint edges, we have Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[g31])≃Ind⁡(K2)∗Ind⁡(K2)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}])\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(K_{2})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(K_{2}), that is, Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[g31])≃𝕊1\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}])\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1}. Similarly, N⁡(b1)⊆N⁡(b3)∩N⁡(g11)∩N⁡(g21)N(b_{1})\subseteq N(b_{3})\cap N(g_{11})\cap N(g_{21}) in the graph B0,5∖N⁡[b6]B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{6}], which implies that Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[b6])≃Ind⁡(B0,5∖(N⁡[b6]∪{b3,g11,g21}))\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{6}])\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus(N[b_{6}]\cup\{b_{3},g_{11},g_{21}\})). Since the graph B0,5∖(N⁡[b6]∪{b3,g11,g21})B_{0,5}\setminus(N[b_{6}]\cup\{b_{3},g_{11},g_{21}\}) is isomorphic to the complete graph K2K_{2}, we have Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[b6])≃𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{6}])\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0}. Therefore, using the fact that Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[g31])≃𝕊1\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{31}])\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1} and Ind⁡(B0,5∖N⁡[b6])≃𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5}\setminus N[b_{6}])\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0}, we get Ind⁡(B0,5)≃𝕊1∨𝕊2\mathrm{Ind}(B_{0,5})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1}\vee\mathbb{S}^{2}.

Now, assume n≥1n\geq 1. Since N⁡(b2)⊆N⁡(b5)N(b_{2})\subseteq N(b_{5}) in the graph Bn,5B_{n,5} (see Figure 14), using Proposition 2.3, we get Ind⁡(Bn,5)≃Ind⁡(Bn,5∖b5)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}\setminus b_{5}). Observe that [b4,g41;b2][b_{4},g_{41};b_{2}] is an edge-invariant triplet in Bn,5∖b5B_{n,5}\setminus b_{5}. Therefore, by Proposition 2.5, we have Ind⁡(Bn,5)≃Ind⁡(Bn,51)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{1}), where Bn,51≔(Bn,5∖b5)+{b4​g41}B_{n,5}^{1}\coloneq(B_{n,5}\setminus b_{5}){+}\{b_{4}g_{41}\} (see Figure 22(a)). Furthermore, [b4,g31;b2][b_{4},g_{31};b_{2}] is an edge-invariant triplet in Bn,51B_{n,5}^{1}, and [b1,b4;b6][b_{1},b_{4};b_{6}] is an edge-invariant triplet in Bn,51+{b4​g31}B_{n,5}^{1}+\{b_{4}g_{31}\}. Let Bn,52≔(Bn,51+{b4​g31})−{b1​b4}B_{n,5}^{2}\coloneqq(B_{n,5}^{1}{+}\{b_{4}g_{31}\})-\{b_{1}b_{4}\} (see Figure 22(b)). Then, Ind⁡(Bn,5)≃Ind⁡(Bn,52)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{2}). Since N⁡(b1)⊆N⁡(b6)N(b_{1})\subseteq N(b_{6}) in Bn,52B_{n,5}^{2}, using Proposition 2.3, we have Ind⁡(Bn,52)≃Ind⁡(Bn,52∖b6)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{2}\setminus b_{6}). Note that the graph Bn,52∖b6B_{n,5}^{2}\setminus b_{6} comprises two connected components: an edge b1​b2b_{1}b_{2} and another component that we denote by Bn,53B_{n,5}^{3} (see Figure 22(c)). This implies that Ind⁡(Bn,5)≃Ind⁡(Bn,52)≃Σ​Ind​(Bn,53)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}). Observe that Ind⁡(Bn,53∖N⁡[b4])∗{b3}\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus N[b_{4}])*\{b_{3}\} is a subcomplex of Ind⁡(Bn,53∖b4)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus b_{4}), which implies that the inclusion map Ind⁡(Bn,53∖N⁡[b4])↪Ind⁡(Bn,53∖b4)\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus N[b_{4}])\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus b_{4}) is null homotopic. Therefore, by Proposition 2.2, we get

Ind⁡(Bn,53)≃Ind⁡(Bn,53∖b4)∨Σ​Ind​(Bn,53∖N⁡[b4]).\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus b_{4})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus N[b_{4}]).

Note that, the graph Bn,53∖N⁡[b4]B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus N[b_{4}] is isomorphic to the graph Λn−1,5\Lambda_{n-1,5}, and the graph Bn,53∖b4B_{n,5}^{3}\setminus b_{4} is isomorphic to Cn,5C_{n,5} (refer to Figure 11 and Figure 15). Claim 5.8.
Ind⁡(Cn,5)≃{𝕊1if n=0,∨3𝕊2if n=1,Σ3​Ind​(An−2,5)​⋁Σ2​Ind​(En−1,5)​⋁Σ3​Ind​(Fn−2,5)if n≥2.\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{1}&\text{if $n=0$,}\\ \vee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{2}&\text{if $n=1$,}\\ \Sigma^{3}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-2,5})\bigvee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(E_{n-1,5})\bigvee\Sigma^{3}\mathrm{Ind}(F_{n-2,5})&\text{if $n\geq 2$.}\end{cases}
Proof.

Let n=0n=0. Since N⁡(g11)⊆N⁡(g31)N(g_{11})\subseteq N(g_{31}) in the graph C0,5C_{0,5} (see Figure 15), using Proposition 2.3, we conclude that Ind⁡(C0,5)≃Ind⁡(C0,5∖g31)\mathrm{Ind}(C_{0,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{0,5}\setminus g_{31}). However, the graph C0,5∖g31C_{0,5}\setminus g_{31} consists of exactly two disjoint edges. Therefore, Ind⁡(C0,5)≃𝕊1.\mathrm{Ind}(C_{0,5})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1}.

Now, assume n≥1n\geq 1. Since N⁡(g11)⊆N⁡(g22)N(g_{11})\subseteq N(g_{22}) in the graph Cn,5C_{n,5}, by Proposition 2.3, we have Ind⁡(Cn,5)≃Ind⁡(Cn,5∖g22)\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}\setminus g_{22}). We denote the graph Cn,5∖g22C_{n,5}\setminus g_{22} by Cn,51C_{n,5}^{1}. Since c1c_{1} is a simplicial vertex and N⁡(c1)={g31,g41}N(c_{1})=\{g_{31},g_{41}\} in Cn,51C_{n,5}^{1}, using Proposition 2.4, we get that

(5.7) Ind⁡(Cn,51)≃Σ​Ind​(Cn,51∖N⁡[g31])∨Σ​Ind​(Cn,51∖N⁡[g41]).{}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{1})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{31}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{41}]).

Let Cn,52≔Cn,51∖N⁡[g41]C_{n,5}^{2}\coloneqq C_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{41}] (see Figure 23(a)). Observe that [g13,g32;g11][g_{13},g_{32};g_{11}] and [g23,g32;g11][g_{23},g_{32};g_{11}] are edge-invariant triplets in Cn,52C_{n,5}^{2} and Cn,52+{g13​g32}C_{n,5}^{2}{+}\{g_{13}g_{32}\}, respectively. Therefore, using Proposition 2.5, Ind(Cn,52)≃Ind(Cn,52+{g13g32,\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2}{+}\{g_{13}g_{32}, g23g32})g_{23}g_{32}\}). Analogously, [g12,g13;g21][g_{12},g_{13};g_{21}] and [g12,g23;g21][g_{12},g_{23};g_{21}] form edge invariant triplets in Cn,52+{g13​g32,g32​g23}C_{n,5}^{2}+\{g_{13}g_{32},g_{32}g_{23}\} and Cn,52+{g13​g32,g32​g23}−{g12​g13}C_{n,5}^{2}+\{g_{13}g_{32},g_{32}g_{23}\}-\{g_{12}g_{13}\}, respectively. Thus, we have Ind⁡(Cn,52+{g13​g32,g32​g23})≃Ind⁡(Cn,52+{g13​g32,g32​g23}−{g12​g13,g12​g23})\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2}+\{g_{13}g_{32},g_{32}g_{23}\})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2}+\{g_{13}g_{32},g_{32}g_{23}\}-\{g_{12}g_{13},g_{12}g_{23}\}). We denote the graph Cn,52+{g13​g32,g32​g23}−{g12​g13,g12​g23}C_{n,5}^{2}+\{g_{13}g_{32},g_{32}g_{23}\}-\{g_{12}g_{13},g_{12}g_{23}\} by Cn,53C_{n,5}^{3}, depicted in Figure 23(b). Then, Ind⁡(Cn,52)≃Ind⁡(Cn,53)\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{3}). Furthermore, N⁡(g12)⊆N⁡(g21)N(g_{12})\subseteq N(g_{21}) in Cn,53C_{n,5}^{3}. Therefore, by Proposition 2.3, we have Ind⁡(Cn,53)≃Ind⁡(Cn,53∖g21)\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{3}\setminus g_{21}). Observe that the graph Cn,53∖g21C_{n,5}^{3}\setminus g_{21} consists of two connected components, one of which is an edge g11​g12g_{11}g_{12} and the other connected component is isomorphic to En−1,5E_{n-1,5} (see Figure 17). Thus, we have

(5.8) Ind⁡(Cn,52)≃Σ​Ind​(En−1,5).{}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(E_{n-1,5}).

On the other hand, let Cn,54≔Cn,51∖N⁡[g31]C_{n,5}^{4}\coloneqq C_{n,5}^{1}\setminus N[g_{31}] (see Figure 23(c)). Since g11g_{11} is a simplicial vertex in Cn,54C_{n,5}^{4} with a unique neighbour g12g_{12}, by Proposition 2.4, we have Ind⁡(Cn,54)≃Σ​Ind​(Cn,54∖N⁡[g12])\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{4})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{12}]). Let Cn,55≔Cn,54∖N⁡[g12]C_{n,5}^{5}\coloneq C_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{12}] (see Figure 23(d)). Now, for n=1n=1, we have C1,55≃K3C_{1,5}^{5}\simeq K_{3}. Therefore, from (5.7) and (5.8), we get that Ind⁡(C1,5)≃Σ2​Ind​(E0,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(K3)\mathrm{Ind}(C_{1,5})\simeq\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(E_{0,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(K_{3}). Since Ind⁡(E0,5)≃𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(E_{0,5})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0} (using Claim 5.10) and Ind⁡(K3)≃𝕊0∨𝕊0\mathrm{Ind}(K_{3})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{0}\vee\mathbb{S}^{0}, we have Ind(C1,5)≃∨3𝕊2\mathrm{Ind}(C_{1,5})\simeq\vee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{2}.

Let n≥2n\geq 2. Since g42g_{42} is a simplicial vertex and N⁡(g42)={g33,g43}N(g_{42})=\{g_{33},g_{43}\} in Cn,55C_{n,5}^{5}, Proposition 2.4 provides us

Ind⁡(Cn,55)≃Σ​Ind​(Cn,55∖N⁡[g33])∨Σ​Ind​(Cn,55∖N⁡[g43]).\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{5})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{5}\setminus N[g_{33}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{5}\setminus N[g_{43}]).

However, the graph Cn,55∖N⁡[g33]C_{n,5}^{5}\setminus N[g_{33}] is isomorphic to the graph An−2,5A_{n-2,5} and the graph Cn,55∖N⁡[g43]C_{n,5}^{5}\setminus N[g_{43}] is isomorphic to Fn−2,5F_{n-2,5} (refer to Figure 13 and Figure 18). Therefore, we have

(5.9) Ind⁡(Cn,54)≃Σ​Ind​(Cn,55)≃Σ2​Ind​(An−2,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(Fn−2,5),{}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{4})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n,5}^{5})\simeq\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-2,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(F_{n-2,5}),

which, along with (5.7) and (5.8) gives the required homotopy equivalence. ∎

Claim 5.9.
Ind⁡(Dn,5)≃{∨2𝕊1if n=0,∨3𝕊2if n=1,Σ3​Ind​(Λn−2,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(En−1,5)∨Σ2​Ind​(En−1,5)if n≥2.\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\vee^{2}\mathbb{S}^{1}&\text{if $n=0$,}\\ \vee^{3}\mathbb{S}^{2}&\text{if $n=1$,}\\ \Sigma^{3}\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{n-2,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(E_{n-1,5})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(E_{n-1,5})&\text{if $n\geq 2$.}\end{cases}
Proof.

First, let n=0n=0. Since g11g_{11} is a simplicial vertex in D0,5D_{0,5} (see Figure 16) with N⁡(g11)={g21,d1}N(g_{11})=\{g_{21},d_{1}\}, we get Ind⁡(D0,5)≃Σ​Ind​(D0,5∖N⁡[g21])∨Σ​Ind​(D0,5∖N⁡[d1]).\mathrm{Ind}(D_{0,5})\simeq\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(D_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{21}])\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(D_{0,5}\setminus N[d_{1}]). However, both the graphs D0,5∖N⁡[g21]D_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{21}], and D0,5∖N⁡[d1]D_{0,5}\setminus N[d_{1}] are isomorphic to the complete graph K2K_{2}. Therefore, both Ind⁡(D0,5∖N⁡[g21])\mathrm{Ind}(D_{0,5}\setminus N[g_{21}]) and Ind⁡(D0,5∖N⁡[d1])\mathrm{Ind}(D_{0,5}\setminus N[d_{1}]) are homotopy equivalent to 𝕊0\mathbb{S}^{0}. Hence the result.

Now, assume n≥1n\geq 1. Observe that [g31,g12;d1][g_{31},g_{12};d_{1}] and [g21,g42;d2][g_{21},g_{42};d_{2}] are edge-invariant triplets in Dn,5D_{n,5} (see Figure 16) and Dn,5+{g31​g12}D_{n,5}{+}\{g_{31}g_{12}\}, respectively. Hence by using Proposition 2.5, we have Ind⁡(Dn,5)≃Ind⁡(Dn,5+{g31​g12,g21​g42})\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}{+}\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{21}g_{42}\}). Furthermore, [d1,g21;g41][d_{1},g_{21};g_{41}] and [d2,g31;g11][d_{2},g_{31};g_{11}] are edge-invariant triplets in Dn,5+{g31​g12,g21​g42}D_{n,5}{+}\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{21}g_{42}\} and (Dn,5+{g31​g12,g21​g42})−{d1​g21}(D_{n,5}{+}\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{21}g_{42}\})-\{d_{1}g_{21}\}, respectively. Let Dn,51D_{n,5}^{1} be the graph that we obtain after removing the edges d1​g21d_{1}g_{21} and d2​g31d_{2}g_{31} from Dn,5+{g31​g12,g21​g42}D_{n,5}{+}\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{21}g_{42}\} (see Figure 24(a)). Then, it follows from Proposition 2.5 that Ind⁡(Dn,5)≃Ind⁡(Dn,51)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{1}).

Now, we proceed with Dn,51D_{n,5}^{1}. Observe that [g21,g41;d1][g_{21},g_{41};d_{1}], [g12,g41;d1][g_{12},g_{41};d_{1}], and [d2,g41;g11][d_{2},g_{41};g_{11}] are edge-invariant triplets in the graphs Dn,51D_{n,5}^{1}, Dn,51+{g21​g41}D_{n,5}^{1}+\{g_{21}g_{41}\}, and Dn,51+{g21​g41,g12​g41}D_{n,5}^{1}+\{g_{21}g_{41},g_{12}g_{41}\}, respectively. Let Dn,52≔(Dn,51+{g21​g41,g41​g12})−{d2​g41}D_{n,5}^{2}\coloneq(D_{n,5}^{1}+\{g_{21}g_{41},g_{41}g_{12}\})-\{d_{2}g_{41}\} (see Figure 24(b)). Then Proposition 2.5 implies that Ind⁡(Dn,51)≃Ind⁡(Dn,52)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{1})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{2}). Note that N⁡(d2)⊆N⁡(g11)N(d_{2})\subseteq N(g_{11}) in the resultant graph Dn,52D_{n,5}^{2}. Therefore, from Proposition 2.3, we have Ind⁡(Dn,52)≃Ind⁡(Dn,52∖g11)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11}). Since [g12,g33;g21][g_{12},g_{33};g_{21}], and [g12,g43;g21][g_{12},g_{43};g_{21}] are edge-invariant triplets in the graphs Dn,52∖g11D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11} and (Dn,52∖g11)+{g12​g33}(D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11})+\{g_{12}g_{33}\}, respectively, we get Ind⁡(Dn,52∖g11)≃Ind⁡((Dn,52∖g11)+{g12​g33,g12​g43})\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}((D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11})+\{g_{12}g_{33},g_{12}g_{43}\}). Let us take Dn,53≔(Dn,52∖g11)+{g12​g33,g12​g43}D_{n,5}^{3}\coloneq(D_{n,5}^{2}\setminus g_{11})+\{g_{12}g_{33},g_{12}g_{43}\} (see Figure 24(c)). Then, Ind⁡(Dn,52)≃Ind⁡(Dn,53)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{2})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{3}). Furthermore, [g31,g12;g42][g_{31},g_{12};g_{42}] and [g12,g41;g32][g_{12},g_{41};g_{32}] are edge-invariant triplets in the graphs Dn,53D_{n,5}^{3} and Dn,53−{g31​g12}D_{n,5}^{3}-\{g_{31}g_{12}\}, respectively. Hence Ind⁡(Dn,53)≃Ind⁡(Dn,53−{g31​g12,g12​g41})\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{3}-\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{12}g_{41}\}). Let us denote the graph Dn,53−{g31​g12,g12​g41}D_{n,5}^{3}-\{g_{31}g_{12},g_{12}g_{41}\} by Dn,54D_{n,5}^{4} (see Figure 24(d)). Then, Ind⁡(Dn,53)≃Ind⁡(Dn,54)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{3})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}).

Observe that Ind⁡(Dn,54∖N⁡[g21])∗{g41}⊆Ind⁡(Dn,54∖g21)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{21}])*\{g_{41}\}\subseteq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21}), i.e., Ind⁡(Dn,54∖N⁡[g21])\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{21}]) is contractible in Ind⁡(Dn,54∖g21)\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21}). Therefore, Proposition 2.2 implies that

(5.10) Ind⁡(Dn,54)≃Ind⁡(Dn,54∖g21)∨Σ​Ind​(Dn,54∖N⁡[g21])≃Ind⁡(Dn,54∖g21)∨Σ2​Ind​(En−1,5),{}\begin{split}\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4})&\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21})\vee\Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{21}])\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21})\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(E_{n-1,5}),\end{split}

where the second homotopy equivalence holds because the graph Dn,54∖N⁡[g21]D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus N[g_{21}] has two connected components; one component is an edge d1​d2d_{1}d_{2} and the other component is isomorphic to the graph En−1,5E_{n-1,5} (see Figure 17).

Now, consider the graph Dn,54∖g21D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21}. Since N⁡(g41)⊆N⁡(g32)N(g_{41})\subseteq N(g_{32}) in Dn,54∖g21D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21}, we have Ind⁡(Dn,54∖g21)≃Ind⁡(Dn,54∖{g21,g32})\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus g_{21})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus\{g_{21},g_{32}\}). Furthermore, [g22,g33;g41][g_{22},g_{33};g_{41}] and [g22,g43;g41][g_{22},g_{43};g_{41}] are edge-invariant triplets in the graphs Dn,54∖{g21,g32}D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus\{g_{21},g_{32}\} and (Dn,54∖{g21,g32})+{g22​g33}(D_{n,5}^{4}\setminus\{g_{21},g_{32}\})+\{g_{22}g_{33}\}, respectively. Claim 5.11.
Ind⁡(Fn,5)≃{∨4𝕊1if n=0,Σ​Ind​(Bn−1,5)∨(⋁2Σ2​Ind​(Cn−1,5))∨Σ2​Ind​(Dn−1,5)​if n≥1.\mathrm{Ind}(F_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\vee^{4}\mathbb{S}^{1}\hskip 207.7052pt\text{if $n=0$},\\ \Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(B_{n-1,5})\vee\left({\bigvee}^{2}\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(C_{n-1,5})\right)\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n-1,5})\ \text{if $n\geq 1$}.\end{cases}

Theorem 5.12.

For any graph Gn,5∈{Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5:n≥0}G_{n,5}\in\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}:n\geq 0\}, Ind⁡(Gn,5)\mathrm{Ind}(G_{n,5}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

Proof.

For any graph G0,5∈{Γ0,5,Λ0,5,A0,5,B0,5,C0,5,D0,5,E0,5,F0,5}G_{0,5}\in\{\Gamma_{0,5},\Lambda_{0,5},A_{0,5},B_{0,5},C_{0,5},D_{0,5},E_{0,5},F_{0,5}\}, Ind⁡(G0,5)\mathrm{Ind}(G_{0,5}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres from Claims 5.4 to 5.11. Now using induction on nn, and recursive relations established in Claims 5.4 to 5.11, we conclude that, for any graph Gn,5∈{Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5:n≥0}G_{n,5}\in\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}:n\geq 0\}, Ind⁡(Gn,5)\mathrm{Ind}(G_{n,5}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres. ∎

5.2  Independence complex of Γ~n,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5}

Recall that for n≥0n\geq 0, the line graph of P2​n+3×P5P_{2n+3}\times P_{5} comprises of two connected components Λn,5\Lambda_{n,5} and Γ~n,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5} (see Figures 11 and 12). The computation of Ind⁡(Γ~n,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5}) follows a similar approach as that of Ind⁡(Γn,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5}). The intermediary graphs occurring during the computation of Ind⁡(Γ~n,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5}) resemble those defined in Section 5.1.1, with an inclusion of certain additional vertices and edges. For each Hn,5∈{Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5}H_{n,5}\in\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}\}, where n∈ℕ∪{0}n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, we define

V⁡(H~n,5)=V⁡(Hn,5)∪{g1 2​n+2,g2 2​n+2,g3 2​n+2,g4 2​n+2},E⁡(H~n,5)=E(Hn,5)∪{gi​ 2​n+1gi​ 2​n+2:i=1,2,3,4}∪{gi​ 2​n+2gi+1 2​n+2:i=1,2,3}∪{g2 2​n+1​g3 2​n+2,g3 2​n+1​g2 2​n+2}.\begin{split}V(\widetilde{H}_{n,5})=&V(H_{n,5})\cup\{g_{1\,2n+2},g_{2\,2n+2},g_{3\,2n+2},g_{4\,2n+2}\},\\ E(\widetilde{H}_{n,5})=&E(H_{n,5})\cup\{g_{i\,2n+1}g_{i\,2n+2}:i=1,2,3,4\}\cup\{g_{i\,2n+2}g_{i+1\,2n+2}:i=1,2,3\}\\ &\cup\{g_{2\,2n+1}g_{3\,2n+2},g_{3\,2n+1}g_{2\,2n+2}\}.\end{split}

In this section, we compute the independence complexes of graphs Γ~n,5,Λ~n,5,A~n,5,B~n,5,\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5},\widetilde{\Lambda}_{n,5},\widetilde{A}_{n,5},\widetilde{B}_{n,5}, C~n,5\widetilde{C}_{n,5}, D~n,5,E~n,5\widetilde{D}_{n,5},\widetilde{E}_{n,5}, and F~n,5\widetilde{F}_{n,5}. In computing the independence complexes of these graphs, as discussed in Section 5.1.2, our approach focuses on performing computations primarily on one end (the leftmost part) of the graph while keeping the other end (the rightmost part) fixed. Notably, for n≥1n\geq 1, observe that the left ends of the graphs Hn,5H_{n,5} and H~n,5\widetilde{H}_{n,5} coincide, where Hn,5∈{Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5}H_{n,5}\in\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}\}. This observation suggests a method for computing the independence complexes of graphs Γ~n,5,Λ~n,5,A~n,5,B~n,5,C~n,5,D~n,5,E~n,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5},\widetilde{\Lambda}_{n,5},\widetilde{A}_{n,5},\widetilde{B}_{n,5},\widetilde{C}_{n,5},\widetilde{D}_{n,5},\widetilde{E}_{n,5}, and F~n,5\widetilde{F}_{n,5} using a similar strategy to that outlined in Section 5.1.2. Furthermore, for n≥1n\geq 1, these intermediary graphs adhere to a similar recurrence relation as those described in the preceding section. Since the base graphs of these intermediary graphs are completely different from the graphs in Section 5.1.1, we provide the complete computations for base cases. Also, we give the explicit recurrence relation for each graph and higher values of nn.

Since the graph C~1,55∖g33\widetilde{C}_{1,5}^{5}\setminus g_{33} is a path on 66 vertices, Ind⁡(C~1,55)≃𝕊1\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{C}_{1,5}^{5})\simeq\mathbb{S}^{1}. For n≥1n\geq 1, the relation for Ind⁡(F~n,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{F}_{n,5}) follows from a similar argument as that of Claim 5.11. Thus,

    (5.27) Ind⁡(F~n,5)≃{𝕊2∨𝕊2for n=0,Σ​Ind​(B~n−1,5)​⋁Σ2​Ind​(C~n−1,5)​⋁Σ2​Ind​(C~n−1,5)​⋁Σ2​Ind​(D~n−1,5)for n≥1.\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{F}_{n,5})\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{S}^{2}\vee\mathbb{S}^{2}&\text{for $n=0$,}\\ \Sigma\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{B}_{n-1,5})\bigvee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{C}_{n-1,5})\bigvee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{C}_{n-1,5})\bigvee\Sigma^{2}\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{D}_{n-1,5})&\text{for $n\geq 1$.}\end{cases}
Theorem 5.13.

For any graph G~n,5∈{Γ~n,5,Λ~n,5,A~n,5,B~n,5,C~n,5,D~n,5,E~n,5,F~n,5:n≥0}\widetilde{G}_{n,5}\in\{\widetilde{\Gamma}_{n,5},\widetilde{\Lambda}_{n,5},\widetilde{A}_{n,5},\widetilde{B}_{n,5},\widetilde{C}_{n,5},\widetilde{D}_{n,5},\widetilde{E}_{n,5},\widetilde{F}_{n,5}:n\geq 0\}, Ind⁡(G~n,5)\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{G}_{n,5}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

Proof.

The result follows from (5.20) to (5.27), Theorem 5.12 and induction on nn. ∎

5.3  Homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})

In this section, we conclude the homotopy type of 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5}). We also determine the maximum and minimum dimensions of the spheres occurring in the homotopy type of the independence complexes of the graphs in {Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5}, Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5}C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}\}.

Theorem 5.14.

For n≥2n\geq 2, 𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5}) is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

Proof.

Case 1: If nn is even, i.e., n=2​kn=2k for some positive integer kk, then Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5} comprises of two isomorphic connected components whose line graphs are isomorphic to Γk−1,5\Gamma_{k-1,5}. Thus,

𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)≃Ind⁡(Γk−1,5)∗Ind⁡(Γk−1,5).\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{k-1,5})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{k-1,5}).

Now, the result follows from Theorem 5.12.

Case 2: If nn is odd, i.e., n=2​k+1n=2k+1 for some positive integer kk, then Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5} comprises of two non-isomorphic connected components with corresponding line graphs isomorphic to Λk−1,5\Lambda_{k-1,5} and Γ~k−1,5\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k-1,5}. Thus,

𝖬⁡(Pn×P5)≃Ind⁡(Λk−1,5)∗Ind⁡(Γ~k−1,5).\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{5})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Lambda_{k-1,5})\ast\mathrm{Ind}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_{k-1,5}).

The result follows from Theorems 5.12 and 5.13. ∎

Proposition 5.15.

For n≥0n\geq 0, the maximum and minimum dimension of the spheres in the homotopy type of the independence complexes of graphs in {Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5,Cn,5,\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5},C_{n,5}, Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5}D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}\} are given in Table 6 and Table 7, respectively.

Proof.

We prove the statement by using induction on nn for the graphs in {Γn,5,Λn,5,An,5,Bn,5\{\Gamma_{n,5},\Lambda_{n,5},A_{n,5},B_{n,5}, Cn,5,Dn,5,En,5,Fn,5}C_{n,5},D_{n,5},E_{n,5},F_{n,5}\} for n≥0n\geq 0. The statement holds for n=0n=0 from Claims 5.4 to 5.11. Assume that the statement holds for all non-negative integers less than nn. For Γn,5\Gamma_{n,5}, implies that the statement holds for n=1n=1 as well. Further, for n≥2n\geq 2, we have

(5.28) Ind(Γn,5)≃∨2Σ3Ind(Dn−2,5)∨Σ3Ind(An−2,5).{}\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5})\simeq{\vee}^{2}\Sigma^{3}\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n-2,5})\vee\Sigma^{3}\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-2,5}).

Therefore, d𝑚𝑎𝑥​(Ind⁡(Γn,5))d_{\mathit{max}}(\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5})) is given by

Let n≡0​(mod​  4)n\equiv 0\,({\mathrm{mod\;\,}4}). Then n−2n-2 is congruent to 22 modulo 44. By the induction hypothesis, we have

d𝑚𝑎𝑥​(Ind⁡(Γn,5))=max⁡{3+(7​(n−4)/4+4),3+(7​(n−4)/4+4)}=7​(n4).\begin{split}d_{\mathit{max}}(\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5}))=&\max\{3+(\nicefrac{{7(n-4)}}{{4}}+4),3+(\nicefrac{{7(n-4)}}{{4}}+4)\}\\ =&7\left(\frac{n}{4}\right).\end{split}

The proof or n≡1,2,3​(mod​  4)n\equiv 1,2,3\,({\mathrm{mod\;\,}4}) follows similarly.

On the other hand, d𝑚𝑖𝑛​(Ind⁡(Γn,5))d_{\mathit{min}}(\mathrm{Ind}(\Gamma_{n,5})) is given by

min{3+d𝑚𝑖𝑛(Ind(An−2,5)),3+d𝑚𝑖𝑛(Ind(Dn−2,5))}.\begin{split}\min\{&3+d_{\mathit{min}}(\mathrm{Ind}(A_{n-2,5})),3+d_{\mathit{min}}(\mathrm{Ind}(D_{n-2,5}))\}.\end{split}

For n≡0​(mod​  5)n\equiv 0\,({\mathrm{mod\;\,}5}), n−2n-2 is congruent to 33 modulo 55. Therefore, using the induction hypothesis, we have

6 Future Directions

We proved that for n≥3n\geq 3 and 3≤m≤53\leq m\leq 5, the matching complex of Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres. For m=3m=3, we explicitly compute the number and dimension of spheres appearing in the wedge. Further, for m∈{4,5}m\in\{4,5\}, we have given the minimum and maximum dimension of spheres appearing in the wedge in 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{m}). This exploration naturally leads to the following question:

Question 6.1.

Can we determine the dimensions of the spheres appearing in the wedge representing the homotopy types of the matching complexes of categorical products Pn×P4P_{n}\times P_{4} and Pn×P5P_{n}\times P_{5}?

Based on the main result of this article and our computer-based computations, we propose the following:

Conjecture 6.2.

For n≥3n\geq 3 and m≥6m\geq 6, the matching complex of categorical product Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres.

For odd mm and nn, one of the components of Pn×PmP_{n}\times P_{m} is an induced subgraph of Pn​□​PmP_{n}\Box P_{m} (see Figure 1). Since the homotopy type of the matching complexes of Pn​□​PmP_{n}\Box P_{m} is not known for m≥3m\geq 3, it will be interesting to see if there is any relation between the topology of 𝖬⁡(Pn×Pn)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\times P_{n}) and 𝖬⁡(Pn​□​Pm)\mathsf{M}(P_{n}\Box P_{m}).

Question 6.3.

Is there any correlation between the matching complexes of the cartesian product of path graphs and those of the categorical product of path graphs?
